In a decentralized learning environment, a novel approach called Central Server Free Federated Learning (CSFFL) is proposed for social networks with a single-sided trust model. This approach eliminates the need for a central server, enabling the aggregation of model updates without compromising data privacy. A key challenge in implementing CSFFL is the lack of a trusted central server, which is addressed by utilizing a secure multi-party computation protocol to ensure model privacy. A proposed solution involves a hierarchical tree structure, where clusters are grouped into a forest, and the aggregation of local models within each cluster is performed using the SMC protocol. This approach is shown to be efficient, with a time complexity of O(log^2(n)), where n is the number of clients. Furthermore, a proposed algorithm, Hierarchical CSFFL, is shown to be effective in achieving accurate model updates with a high degree of accuracy.

In this study, we explore the application of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to the task of short-text classification, which is particularly challenging due to the scarcity of features in short texts. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that combines RNNs and CNNs to learn sequential representations of short texts. Our method involves two stages: first, we utilize a CNN to generate feature representations of individual words, followed by an RNN that models the temporal dependencies between these features. In the second stage, we employ the RNN's hidden state as input to a CNN, which then generates a final feature representation for classification. Our approach is evaluated on two real-world datasets, where it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

The analytical formulation of a telecentric etalon is developed, enabling the calculation of its properties and the design of its optical configuration. This formulation is applied to the analysis of a specific etalon, which was designed for the ESPRESSO instrument, and demonstrates its potential for modeling and design purposes.

A matching in a bipartite graph consisting of vertices U and V linked by edges can be considered 'compatible' if it adheres to the condition that for every vertex v in V, the vertices in U that are connected to it are a subset of the vertices it is connected to. This concept of compatible matchings has been found to be applicable in various real-world scenarios, such as the allocation of students to schools based on their preferred schools and the distribution of candidates to political parties based on their ideologies. This paper delves into the complexity of finding compatible matchings in bipartite graphs, as well as the allocation of students to schools based on their preferred schools and the distribution of candidates to political parties based on their ideologies.

The codelet model is a programming abstraction that enables the creation of 
customizable, high-performance, and efficient code for diverse hardware accelerators.
This model is particularly beneficial for heterogeneous systems comprising multiple 
chiplets, which are smaller components within a larger chip. Each chiplet is a separate 
silicon entity, and codelets facilitate the distribution of tasks among them, maximizing 
throughput while minimizing communication overhead. The codelet model is designed to 
be hardware-agnostic, allowing developers to write efficient code for various accelerators 
and systems without needing to modify the underlying hardware.

A novel presmoothing technique is introduced to enhance estimation in the semiparametric mixture cure model. This approach yields a convergent and asymptotically normal estimator for the cure fraction, and the obtained results facilitate the estimation of other model parameters. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through a simulation study and an empirical analysis of breast cancer data.

In-memory computing (IMC) has the potential to significantly boost computing efficiency by integrating processing and memory capabilities. However, this architecture also presents new security risks due to the transfer of sensitive data between memory and processing elements. Our research focuses on evaluating the vulnerability of IMC systems to side-channel attacks, specifically targeting the data transmission phase. We developed a novel attack method that exploits the data transmission phase in IMC systems, and our results demonstrate the feasibility of this approach on a real-world IMC system.

A novel approach to constructing polar codes with reduced length is presented, 
wherein the standard polarization process is truncated after a specified number 
of iterations, resulting in a code with a shorter length. The truncated process 
is applied to both the inner and outer code components. Theoretical analysis 
demonstrates that the truncated polarization code achieves a similar error rate 
as the full-length code, provided that the truncation occurs after a sufficient 
number of iterations. The performance of truncated polar codes is evaluated 
through simulations, revealing that they retain the error-correcting efficiency 
of their full-length counterparts, even when shortened to a third of their 
original length.

A novel self-supervised approach to seismic denoising is presented, leveraging the capabilities of a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract noise from seismic data. By utilizing a transfer learning strategy, the network is adapted to identify noise patterns in a specific seismic application, while a self-supervised approach is used to fine-tune the network for optimal performance. This approach is demonstrated through its application to seismic data from the North Sea, where a pre-trained network successfully identifies noise patterns in 2D and 3D seismic data. The results indicate that the network accurately detects noise patterns in 2D and 3D seismic data, while a self-supervised approach further enhances the network's ability to remove noise from the data.

The elastic scattering of charged leptons and antileptons on protons is studied, accounting for the influence of virtual and real photon exchange. A theoretical framework is developed to describe this process, incorporating the electromagnetic form factor of the proton and the associated charge asymmetry. Experimental implications are considered, with a focus on the elastic scattering of polarized leptons and antileptons.

The electronic properties of Sr$_2$IrO$_{4}$ are studied using scanning tunneling spectroscopy, revealing a complex energy spectrum consisting of multiple bands. These bands are identified as resulting from the interaction of electrons with spin-fluctuations, which are generated by the spin-orbit coupling in the material. This interaction causes the formation of a spin-polaron, which is a quasiparticle composed of an electron and a spin-fluctuation. The energy spectrum of this quasiparticle exhibits a characteristic ladder structure, which is a result of the interaction between the spin-fluctuations, and can be described by a theoretical model. The energy spectrum of the spin-polaron exhibits a characteristic pattern of steps, which is a result of the interaction between the spin-fluctuations, and can be described by a theoretical model. A common approach in causal mediation analysis is to use a structural equation model with binary treatment data. However, this approach is limited when dealing with continuous treatment data, as it cannot be modeled. To overcome this limitation, a new method called MCMA is proposed, which uses continuous treatment data to estimate direct and indirect effects. MCMA is based on multiply robust score functions and is shown to be consistent and efficient under certain conditions. Simulation studies and real-world data analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of MCMA in handling missing data and binary treatment limitations.

This special issue of the Journal of Astronomical Telescopes and Instrumentation is a compilation of papers that delve into the current state of starshades, offering a comprehensive analysis of the technology's historical development, its current status, and its potential for future advancements. The papers within this issue are intended to provide a valuable resource for researchers, both those who are new to the field and those who are well-versed in it, as they explore the various aspects of starshades, including their design, construction, and operational capabilities. The papers also examine the challenges associated with the development of starshades, such as the need for specialized manufacturing techniques and the difficulties in testing and validating the technology. Furthermore, this issue touches on the potential applications of starshades, including the study of exoplanetary systems, the formation of stars and planets, and the investigation of the universe's most extreme objects.

This study introduces Robin, a comprehensive online suicidal text dataset that offers a detailed understanding of suicidal behavior. It encompasses 1,111 distinct suicide-related topics, with 1,010 containing explicit references to self-destruction and 101 being indirect. Robin is comprised of 1,111 posts from 1,111 individuals, with 1,010 posts being direct expressions of suicidal intent and 101 being indirect. Robin is notable for its extensive content, with 1,010 posts being direct expressions of suicidal intent and 101 being indirect. We introduce a supersymmetric version of the Schwarzian mechanics, which is derived from a supersymmetric first-order formalism. This approach is based on a superfield action and involves a superderivative, leading to a supersymmetric superderivative formulation. We also explore the superalgebraic structure and present a superfield version of the Schwarzian mechanics, which is equivalent to a supersymmetric superfield version of the first-order mechanics.

This paper explores the difference equation $x_{n+1}=ax^\alpha_{n}+bx^\alpha_{n-1}$, where $0<\alpha \leq2$, and demonstrates that it has bounded solutions under certain conditions, specifically when the initial values fall within a specific range. Furthermore, we examine the practical implications of these solutions in medicine.

We investigate a class of non-linear electrodynamics models, which are derived from a modified Born-Infeld equation. By incorporating a parameter 'a', we analyze the properties of these models, which are then applied to a spherically symmetric black hole solution. The resulting black hole solution is examined in terms of its physical characteristics, including thermodynamic stability and phase transitions. Furthermore, we explore the behavior of these black holes across different parameter spaces and their corresponding phase transitions.

A subset A of non-negative integers has the property that for any two forms f and g, f(x) and g(x) can take on the same value for x in A, except for one specific case where the forms are linear. We prove this under certain conditions and also show that for a specific type of form, almost all subsets of non-negative integers possess this property.

We investigate the magnetic susceptibility of the XY spin chain at finite temperatures, and our findings suggest that it exhibits a scaling behavior with a universal critical point at the quantum critical point. This behavior is in line with the universality principle, and we also discover that the geometric phase in the model displays a similar scaling characteristic.

We've discovered that in the Ising model, a hotter paramagnet takes longer to transition into a ferromagnetic state, a finding that contradicts expectations based on the kinetic Ising model. Notably, our results show that the temperature dependence of the mean spin relaxation time is inverted in the presence of a magnetic field.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic systems, we investigate the phenomenon of pair localization. We focus on a specific model, where the hopping integral between sites decays according to a power-law, and the quasiperiodic potential is represented by a Fibonacci sequence. Our analysis reveals that, for a power-law with an exponent between 0.5 and 1, pairs of sites exhibit localization, whereas single-site localization occurs only for a power-law with an exponent greater than 1. This finding is supported by analytical calculations of the pair localization length and numerical simulations.

The development of multilingual task-oriented dialogue systems is hindered by several challenges, including the scarcity of available data and the need for cross-lingual generalization. To address these obstacles, we examine the role of natural language processing in creating such systems, focusing on the key techniques that enable them to function effectively. We then discuss the difficulties that arise when developing dialogue systems for low-resource languages, where data limitations and the need for cross-lingual generalization pose significant problems. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel approach that leverages pre-trained language models to enhance the performance of low-resource languages. We also highlight the importance of developing and sharing more datasets and models to advance the field of multilingual dialogue systems.

The phenomenon of alternative splicing allows a single gene to produce diverse proteins, which is crucial for life. To understand this process, we analyzed a dataset of RNA sequences from humans and primates, identifying millions of alternative splicing events. By applying a statistical model, we discovered that many of these events are influenced by the presence of multiple transcripts, which can be explained by the presence of multiple promoters or alternative start sites. Additionally, we found that many alternative splicing events are regulated by the presence of alternative stop sites, which can lead to the inclusion or exclusion of specific protein domains. Our analysis also suggests that alternative splicing can be regulated by the presence of alternative promoters, which can be influenced by the presence of specific transcription factors.

In recent years, data protection regulations have become a crucial aspect of IT governance, with various studies examining their implementation. However, the specific role of technical measures in achieving compliance remains understudied. This qualitative study explores how technical measures are used in the implementation of data protection compliance. Our findings indicate that technical measures are employed in all stages of the compliance process, with a focus on data mapping and risk assessment. Furthermore, our research highlights the challenges associated with implementing technical measures, including the need for specialized expertise and the potential for technical measures to be overlooked.

We investigate the patterns of particle arrangement in collisions involving a proton and another nucleus, focusing on the relationships between particles' movement directions. Our analysis reveals that these patterns are influenced by the distribution of quarks within the nucleus, and we find that the distribution of quarks in a triangular shape leads to specific patterns in particle arrangement. Furthermore, we examine how these patterns change when the energy involved in the collision increases and when the nucleus is replaced by a different type of subatomic particle.

The formation of light nuclei in Au-Au collisions at a 3 GeV energy threshold is studied using the STAR detector at RHIC. Data on pion, kaon, and proton multiplicities, as well as light nuclei production, are examined. A comparison of these results to predictions from statistical and coalescence models reveals that thermal models accurately describe particle ratios, but coalescence models better explain light nuclei production trends. Furthermore, coalescence model calculations suggest that light nuclei are primarily formed through the coalescence of protons and neutrons.

The study of exoplanet atmospheres has become a crucial area of research in modern astrophysics, with significant implications for understanding the formation and evolution of these celestial bodies. In this review, we will examine the current understanding of the atmospheres of rocky exoplanets, with a focus on their composition, structure, and potential for hosting life. We will also discuss the current and future missions that will play a pivotal role in advancing our knowledge of these atmospheres.

This paper explores the dispersability of circulant graphs, providing key findings, including the exact dispersability of the icosahedral graph and a circulant graph of 15 vertices with specific edge conditions, as well as the exact solution for a particular case of the circulant dispersal conjecture.

This paper introduces a novel approach to efficiently invert matrices using iterative methods, with a focus on their potential for GPU acceleration. By leveraging the parallel processing capabilities of the iterative methods, we can achieve significant speedup compared to traditional direct inversion techniques. The proposed method is based on the Neumann series and its higher-order variants, with a focus on minimizing computational overhead and maximizing parallelism. The approach is demonstrated through the implementation of a higher-order Neumann-based method, which is shown to be equivalent to a modified inverse power method. The method's performance is evaluated using the inverse of the Laplacian matrix, with a focus on its efficiency and scalability. The results demonstrate the method's potential for achieving high performance on GPU architectures, with a significant speedup compared to traditional direct inversion techniques.

In this research, we investigate the power spectrum of primordial fluctuations during ultra-slow-roll inflation, taking into account the backreaction effect. We utilize the slow-roll parameters and a parameter representing the deviation from slow-roll conditions to express the power spectrum, and we demonstrate that the power spectrum diverges at the onset of ultra-slow-roll inflation. Furthermore, we examine the behavior of the power spectrum under backreaction and slow-roll conditions, and we discuss the implications of our findings for the tensor-to-scalar ratio.

The Refined Assortment Optimization problem is a more complex version of the Assortment Planning problem, taking into account the demand for each product individually. We've developed a new mixed-integer linear programming model that builds on existing work, allowing for more accurate demand forecasting. We've also identified a key property of the optimal solution, which enables the creation of a more efficient optimization model that can solve the problem to optimality. Our proposed model has been tested using real-world data and shown to be more effective than previous approaches.

A new approach to analyzing time-to-event data is introduced, focusing on the impact of a treatment on the time to a specific event. The proposed method, casebase, is based on the number of individuals who experience the event within a set time frame. The analysis involves comparing the distribution of this number across different groups, providing a clear interpretation of the treatment's effect. The casebase method is particularly useful for identifying the time at which the treatment's effect becomes noticeable, as it is less sensitive to the distribution of event times. The casebase method is also more interpretable than traditional survival analysis methods, as it focuses on the number of individuals who experience the event rather than the time to the event. The casebase method is illustrated with a real-world example and compared to other survival analysis methods, including the Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models.

This dissertation focuses on determining the high-precision results of Feynman integrals, crucial for enhancing the accuracy of theoretical predictions in high-energy experiments. These calculations are essential for refining the understanding of fundamental parameters in particle physics. The dissertation delves into the geometric decomposition of Feynman integrals, utilizing differential equations to derive their explicit forms. The approach is applied to various multi-loop Feynman integrals, including those with up to four scales, and demonstrates the method's applicability to generic integrals with arbitrary kinematics. The dissertation also showcases the importance of these calculations in high-precision physics, particularly in the Standard Model and its potential extensions.

The proliferation of data-driven scientific and engineering applications has led to a significant increase in data storage and management demands. To address these challenges, researchers have developed object storage systems as an alternative to traditional file systems, offering improved data management capabilities. However, the effectiveness of object storage systems in meeting the needs of data-intensive applications remains unclear. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a comparative study of the performance of DAOS, an object storage system, and Lustre, a traditional file system, in handling object data. Our evaluation involved a range of object storage and file system operations, including data creation, replication, and access. The results of our experiments indicate that DAOS and Lustre exhibit distinct performance characteristics, with DAOS offering superior performance for certain operations, such as data replication, and Lustre excelling in other areas, like data access.

The increasing adoption of Electric Vehicles (EVs) is driving a surge in demand for public EV charging infrastructure, particularly in the form of parking lots equipped with charging stations. However, the limited availability of these charging stations poses a significant challenge, as it can lead to long wait times for vehicles to access the limited capacity. To mitigate this issue, we propose an online admission control strategy that optimizes the efficient use of charging stations by dynamically adjusting the number of vehicles allowed to park and charge at each station. Our approach is based on a predictive model that forecasts the arrival and departure times of vehicles, allowing us to develop a policy that maximizes the total number of vehicles that can be accommodated by the charging stations. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving higher system utilization and reduced wait times compared to existing methods.

This study explores the construction and existence of linear complementary dual (LCD) codes through the lens of weight distribution polynomials, with a focus on characterizing weight distributions for LCD codes. Building on this, we develop a systematic approach to constructing LCD codes with optimal parameters using a general framework. This method is applied to various scenarios, including the construction of optimal LCD codes in specific dimensions and parameter ranges, and the creation of new LCD codes with unique characteristics.

We demonstrate that classical general relativity can be derived from loop amplitudes, specifically by combining two-loop vacuum amplitudes with diverse boundary conditions and reducing them to a five-dimensional theory. This reduction process involves eliminating extra dimensions through the application of a specific operator, resulting in the emergence of the Einstein-Hilbert action within the resulting theory.

The shift towards renewable energy is a crucial step towards reducing greenhouse gas emissions, but it also leads to increased land use. To assess the impact of this change, we analyzed the effects of different electricity generation scenarios on land use in the western United States. Our research reveals that transitioning to 100% renewable energy by 2050 would result in a significant expansion of solar and wind energy, requiring approximately 1,000 square miles of land per gigawatt of capacity. However, this expansion would be heavily concentrated in areas with suitable resources, such as the Four Corners region, where it could coexist with existing land uses. To minimize the impact on natural habitats, we propose a strategy that prioritizes the development of solar energy in urban areas and wind energy in rural areas. Our findings suggest that this approach would result in a more balanced distribution of renewable energy facilities, with fewer adverse effects on natural environments.

Cluster-randomized trials are frequently employed to assess the efficacy of vaccines in generating herd immunity. This study examines the estimation of causal effects in such trials, focusing on the impact of vaccine distribution on the incidence of target and non-target diseases within clusters. We investigate the feasibility of using naive estimators, which disregard the interdependence of cluster outcomes, and develop a novel weighted estimator that accounts for this correlation. This weighted estimator is shown to be consistent and asymptotically normal, and we derive a correction for naive estimators to improve their performance. Our findings are supported by a simulation study and demonstrated through an analysis of the 2009-2010 influenza season in the United States.

This paper delves into the normalized Laplacian spectral analysis of a fractal network known as the M\"{o}bius octagonal network. By examining the degree distribution and connectivity of this network, we derive the degree sequence and establish a relationship between the degree and normalized Laplacian spectra. Our results show that the eigenvalues of the normalized Laplacian matrix are real and the corresponding eigenvectors are real. We also explore the applications of this network in the fields of random walks and QoS routing.

We introduce a novel contextual linear bandit algorithm that operates in a distributed environment, allowing multiple agents to collectively learn a shared linear model from their individual experiences. The key distinction from existing distributed algorithms lies in our ability to update the model without requiring agents to share context information. This is achieved through the use of a shared model that is updated via a stochastic gradient descent process, with agents communicating only the gradient of their local loss function. Theoretical analysis confirms the algorithm's sublinear regret and its ability to converge to the optimal model.

The integration of electronic health records (EHRs) into clinical decision support systems has become a crucial aspect of healthcare. However, the lack of standardised EHR formats across different healthcare providers hinders the development of such systems. To address this issue, the creation of synthetic EHRs can facilitate the development of healthcare analytics tools. This study focuses on generating synthetic EHRs for patients with cystic fibrosis by examining the relationship between medication and lung function. Using a dataset from the UK Cystic Fibrosis Data Warehouse, the study applies a combination of deep learning and time-series analysis techniques to build a predictive model. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in predicting lung function values based on medication data, with the model achieving a high accuracy of 0.93. The study's findings have the potential to inform the development of clinical decision support systems for cystic fibrosis patients.

The $D^{0} \to K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pm \pi^\mp$ decay is analyzed using the LHCb experiment's $pp$ collision data, collected at 7, 8, and 13 TeV centre-of-mass energies, corresponding to 9 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. The analysis focuses on the $D^{*}(2380)^0$ and $D^{*}(2600)^0$ resonances, and their properties are determined. The analysis also examines the $D^{0} \to K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pm \pi^\mp$ decay mode, and the results are compared to predictions from the quark model.

The novelty and impact of scientific and technological advancements are crucial factors in determining their significance. To address this, we have developed a Python package called Novelpy, which calculates the novelty and disruptiveness of bibliometric and patent data. This open-source package is designed to be easily integrated into various data sources and offers a range of methods for assessing the novelty and disruptiveness of different datasets. In this study, we have applied Novelpy to analyze the novelty and disruptiveness of publications in the field of solar energy, and we have also compared our results with existing methods for evaluating the impact of scientific research.

We've developed a method to precisely control the trajectory of a high-intensity laser beam by leveraging the interaction between two laser pulses. By carefully designing the initial conditions of the pulses, we can achieve a wide range of intensity variations across the beam, including sharp, flat, or curved patterns. This approach offers a versatile tool for manipulating high-intensity laser beams, with potential applications in advanced laser technologies.

This study explores the capabilities of a robotic system to replicate the shot release of a recurve bow used in the Olympic archery event. The research aims to establish a foundation for future investigations into the robot's potential to match human-level performance in this context. The study's findings are presented in conjunction with an overview of the relevant theory and background information.

Cross-domain recommendation systems have gained significant attention in the research community due to their ability to leverage unlabelled data from related domains to improve performance in the target domain. However, existing methods often struggle with balancing the need for accurate and efficient recommendations. This paper presents a novel approach, Dual Metric Learning, which uses a dual metric learning framework to learn a unified embedding space that captures the relationships between items and users across different domains. By employing a dual metric learning strategy, the proposed method effectively addresses the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. Experimental results on three real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

We introduce a novel fragment of the mu-calculus, specifically the asynchronous distributed mu-fragment, which is defined by a specific class of automata. Our characterization of this fragment demonstrates that it is equivalent to the full mu-calculus, allowing for model-theoretic reasoning and decision-making within its scope.

The thermal conductivity of a two-dimensional complex plasma was investigated by analyzing the radial temperature profile in a cylindrical setup, where a heater was placed at the axis and thermalized particles were measured at the edge. By adjusting the ion-to-atom ratio, the layer's behavior was modified from a traditional plasma to a strongly coupled state. The results showed that the layer's thermal conductivity is significantly lower than expected for a traditional plasma, and this reduction is attributed to the layer's two-dimensional nature and the presence of a strongly coupled state.

We investigate the problem of combining data vectors in a linear manner, 
where the vectors may not be ordered. This scenario is relevant in various 
contexts, such as data vector merging and combining data from multiple sources. 
In contrast to the case where vectors are ordered, the fundamental identity 
$1 = (0+1) - (0\cdot1)$ does not hold. Our research focuses on determining the 
existence of linear combinations that achieve a specific objective, and we 
introduce a new concept of "linear combination distance" to facilitate this 
investigation.

In cardio-angiography, X-ray radiation poses a significant risk to both patients and medical professionals. To minimize this risk, we propose a deep learning-based approach to video interpolation, which reduces the frequency of X-ray exposures by one half without compromising image quality.

The future Circular Collider will be a powerful tool for studying the fundamental properties of heavy quarks, offering unparalleled precision in measuring their masses and interactions. However, the complex processes involved in heavy-quark production and decay pose significant challenges for researchers. This article will examine the key advantages and obstacles of using the FCC-ee to investigate heavy quarks, with a particular focus on the tau lepton as a promising area of investigation.

The neutrino floor phenomenon is a significant challenge for the future generation of neutrino experiments, particularly for the DUNE, T2HK, and T2HK+/T2HA experiments. This issue arises from the interactions between tau neutrinos and muon neutrinos, which are influenced by the $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$ gauge boson. In this study, we investigate the impact of the $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$ gauge boson on the neutrino floor, considering various gauge boson masses. Our findings indicate that the neutrino floor is more pronounced when the gauge boson mass is lower, and that the $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$ gauge boson has a significant effect on the neutrino floor, particularly for the DUNE experiment.

We have developed a new model to simulate the ejection of hypervelocity stars from the Galactic Center. Our model takes into account the effects of secular perturbations caused by an intermediate-mass companion star. We have calculated the probability distribution of ejection velocities and directions for a range of orbital parameters and mass ratios. Our results show that the ejection process is sensitive to the orbital parameters and mass ratio of the companion star. We have also found that the ejection process can produce a wide range of ejection velocities and directions, with a significant number of ejections occurring at high velocities. Our model suggests that the ejection process can produce a population of hypervelocity stars with a wide range of ejection velocities and directions, with a significant number of ejections occurring at high velocities.

We investigate a class of multiplicative stochastic differential equations with singular drifts. Our research demonstrates that weak solutions exist and are unique for these equations. The key to our proof lies in the concept of regularization by noise, which involves adding a suitable noise to the underlying problem. The main challenge arises from the fact that the resulting equation is not Markovian, but we overcome this issue by employing a novel coupling method.

We establish that the nonstationary ideal on ω1 is determined by the smallest forcing axiom, namely PD, and this is achieved without relying on the core model theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the PD principle is sufficient to prove that the nonstationary ideal is not definable through any Σ2 formula.

Recent advancements in pre-trained language models have led to significant breakthroughs in natural language processing. However, the challenge remains to adapt these models to new tasks without compromising their performance on existing ones. To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework called Adaptor, which enables the adaptation of pre-trained models to specific tasks without the need for extensive fine-tuning. By leveraging a task's objective function, Adaptor adapts the model's parameters to align with the task's objective, resulting in a more efficient and effective adaptation process. Our experiments demonstrate that Adaptor outperforms existing methods in adapting pre-trained models to multiple tasks, with notable improvements in both task-specific and multi-task settings.

A comprehensive dataset of 12,000 high-quality images containing various traffic signs from around the world has been compiled. This dataset is designed to support the development of robust traffic sign detection and classification systems that can operate effectively across diverse global locations. The dataset's images were sourced from Mapillary's open database, encompassing a wide range of countries, including those in Central and South America, Europe, India, and Southeast Asia. The dataset's images were annotated by hand, including bounding boxes and class labels, and are available for use under an open license. The dataset's performance was evaluated using a combination of state-of-the-art deep learning models, demonstrating the dataset's potential for training accurate traffic sign detection and classification systems. The dataset's code and data can be accessed via a link on GitHub.

Recommender systems based on collaborative filtering have been widely adopted, but traditional methods that rely on explicit user-item interactions are limited by the issue of sparse data. To address this problem, researchers have turned to self-supervised learning, which can learn from implicit user-item interactions without requiring explicit labels. However, current self-supervised learning methods often involve complex models and large amounts of labeled data, making them difficult to implement. To address this problem, we propose a novel self-supervised learning framework called SelfCF, which uses a simple and efficient approach to learn from implicit user-item interactions. By leveraging the strengths of both self-supervised and traditional collaborative filtering methods, SelfCF can learn from a wide range of user-item interactions and improve recommendation accuracy. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SelfCF, which outperforms traditional methods and achieves state-of-the-art results.

We calculate the generalized Tevelev degree of a morphism $f: \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0, \infty\} \to \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{0\}$ given by a degree $d$ map with a single ramification point at infinity, using a formula that generalizes the classical Tevelev degree formula.

We investigate a Dirac semimetal model with both linear and parabolic dispersions, and a band gap. This model is derived from a 3D lattice with a specific symmetry, and its band structure is characterized by a Dirac point with linear and parabolic dispersions, and a band gap. We examine the model's topological properties, and their connection to the band structure. We find that the model's topological classification is based on the Dirac point's location, and the model's behavior is influenced by the band structure. We also analyze the model's behavior under a specific perturbation, and the model's phase diagram.

We examine the dynamics of a slow, semi-stable curve entering and leaving its host halo. Our analysis reveals that the dynamics of the curve's entry and exit points differ significantly. Specifically, we find that the critical velocity required for entry is always greater than that required for exit. Furthermore, we observe that the dynamics of the exit points exhibit a characteristic 'hysteresis loop', which is not present in the entry dynamics.

The LISA mission is set to detect gravitational waves at frequencies as low as 0.1 Hz, which is the domain of second-generation detectors like LIGO and Virgo. However, future ground-based detectors are expected to reach frequencies of 1 kHz, making it possible to detect higher-order modes of gravitational waves. This study focuses on the detectability of these modes, which are influenced by the mass of compact binary sources and the frequency of the waves. The analysis reveals that higher-order modes can be detected with a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 at frequencies of 1 kHz for certain types of binary systems. The study also suggests that higher-order modes may be detectable in third-generation detectors for a wider range of binary systems.

The Gaia space mission has revolutionized the field of exoplanet research by enabling scientists to study the astrometric wobble of stars caused by their orbiting planets. Although Gaia's capabilities are limited to stars with a certain level of brightness, it can still provide valuable insights into the mass of planets orbiting fainter stars. By analyzing the astrometric data of these stars, scientists can gain a better understanding of the mass of the planets orbiting them. In this study, we have developed a new method to estimate the mass of planets orbiting stars with a single astrometric data point. By applying this method to a sample of 12 known planets, we have demonstrated its effectiveness in recovering the mass of the planets. Furthermore, we have applied this method to a sample of 12 transiting planets and found that the mass of the planets can be estimated with a precision of 10-20%. These results suggest that the mass of the planets can be determined with a precision of 10-20% using Gaia's data.

Genetic algorithms are a type of optimization technique inspired by the process of natural selection, employing a combination of crossover and mutation to find optimal solutions. This research aims to investigate the effectiveness of various crossover and selection methods on the 0/1 Knapsack Problem, utilizing genetic algorithms to identify the most suitable approaches. The study compares different types of crossover, including single-point, two-point, and uniform methods, alongside diverse selection methods, including tournament selection and rank selection. The results reveal that the combination of single-point crossover and rank selection yields the most efficient convergence in solving the 0/1 Knapsack Problem.

The task of identifying hate speech on social media has gained significant attention in recent years due to its potential for harm. Despite the efforts of researchers, current methods still struggle to achieve high accuracy. This study aims to improve hate speech detection by leveraging the T5 model and exploring the benefits of using augmented data and ensemble techniques. We conducted experiments using the Hateful Memes dataset and found that the T5 model excelled at hate speech detection, with a macro F1 score of 0.93. To further enhance performance, we developed a two-stage ensemble approach that combined the predictions of T5 and other models, resulting in a macro F1 score of 0.96. Our results demonstrate the potential of T5 and our ensemble methods for effective hate speech detection.

A crucial step in simulating complex atomic interactions within quantum many-body systems is the inclusion of ions, which can significantly impact the system's behavior. However, accurately modeling these ions is challenging due to the complex interactions they involve. To address this issue, researchers have developed a new method that combines the strengths of quantum Monte Carlo and density functional theory to calculate the forces exerted by ions. This approach, which is based on the random phase approximation, has been successfully tested on various systems, including hydrogen, helium, and lithium. The results show that the method accurately reproduces the known properties of these systems, including their binding energies and ionization potentials. Furthermore, the method has been applied to the lithium atom, which is a significant achievement given the difficulty of modeling lithium's complex interactions. The results show that the method accurately reproduces the atom's energy levels and ionization potential.

The 2020 US presidential election was marred by a multitude of claims of voter fraud, which were disseminated through various social media platforms. Despite the claims, there is no substantial evidence to support them. This research paper presents a comprehensive dataset of 2020 US election-related claims, which were shared on Twitter. The dataset comprises two main components: a collection of tweets containing claims, and a set of corresponding ground truth labels. The dataset is unique in its multi-modal nature, combining both textual and image-based claims, which were identified using both manual and automated methods. The dataset is also annotated with relevant metadata, including the type of claim, the source, and the topic. The dataset is publicly available for research purposes.

We demonstrate that for a diffeomorphism with positive Lyapunov exponents, the set of periodic points is dense. This result is derived from the application of our previously established topological emergence theorem.

Recent advancements in Bayesian deep learning have led to the development of highly efficient models capable of accurately assessing their own uncertainty levels. However, these models often fall short in providing comprehensive uncertainty assessments, relying on simplified approximations. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the potential of Monte Carlo dropout to accurately capture the posterior distribution of Bayesian neural networks. By utilizing a neural network to parameterize the posterior distribution, we can generate a diverse set of samples that accurately reflect the uncertainty in the model's predictions. These samples can then be used to create a probabilistic output, enabling the quantification of uncertainty in a more precise manner. To optimize the sampling process, we employ a neural network to parameterize the posterior distribution, allowing us to generate a diverse set of samples that accurately reflect the uncertainty in the model's predictions. These samples can then be used to create a probabilistic output, enabling the quantification of uncertainty in a more precise manner. To optimize the sampling process, we employ a neural network to parameterize the posterior distribution, allowing us to generate a diverse set of samples that accurately reflect the uncertainty in the model's predictions. These samples can then be used to create a probabilistic output, enabling the quantification of uncertainty in a more precise manner.

The Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory is a widely accepted explanation for the non-adiabatic electron transfer reactions in various systems. This theory is a result of a detailed analysis of the rate of transfer, which is calculated by averaging over the paths of the system's quantum states. This paper presents a new approach to this theory, which is based on the concept of instantons in the context of the Euclidean path integral. This formulation provides a more detailed understanding of the theory, which is evident in the fact that it can account for the effects of quantum tunneling. The paper also discusses the limitations of the original theory, which is based on the assumption that the system's energy is a simple function of time.

This research introduces a novel hybrid control design approach, tailored to trajectory control, by integrating two distinct methods: a nonlinear model predictive control and a linear quadratic regulator. The proposed hybrid control design is then applied to a simulated robotic arm, operating within a two-dimensional environment, to demonstrate its effectiveness.

A theoretical framework is developed to explain the significant thermoelectric effect observed in thin-film Heusler alloys, which is attributed to the magnon drag mechanism. This framework is applied to a specific thin-film Heusler alloy, Fe$_2$V$_{0.5}$W$_{0.5}$Al, and the results are compared with experimental data. The theoretical predictions match the experimental results, providing a new understanding of the thermoelectric properties of this material.

The Perfect Sum Problem, a combinatorial issue, seeks to determine the existence of non-negative integer coefficients $x_1, x_2,..., x_n$ that satisfy the equation $x_1 + x_2 +... + x_n = k$ for a given positive integer $n$ and $k$. This problem has been studied extensively, with various solutions proposed for both the general and specific cases. In this paper, a probabilistic approach is presented to solve the Perfect Sum Problem, which is based on the concept of the binomial distribution.

This paper presents a method to determine the highest possible powers that elements within a finite field can be raised to, when those elements are defined using a particular polynomial equation. The result obtained in this study can be utilized to calculate the highest powers that elements within a finite field can be raised to, when those elements are defined using a specific type of polynomial.

In recent years, the use of formal methods in software development has become more prevalent, yet the majority of these methods rely on specialized tools that are inaccessible to the average programmer. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach that enables the analysis of source code using a model checker. By converting source code into a model, we can leverage the capabilities of a model checking tool, specifically UPPAAL, to perform various analyses. In this context, we demonstrate how UPPAAL can be employed to analyze source code, including identifying deadlocks, calculating the number of execution paths, and verifying the reachability of a given state.

A novel method for imaging utilizing metasurfaces is presented, which leverages compressed sensing principles to optimize imaging performance. The approach involves formulating an optimization problem to minimize the scattering from a metasurface, with the goal of reconstructing a target object using a limited number of measurements. The problem is solved using a gradient-based method, which allows for the simultaneous optimization of both the metasurface and the reconstructed object. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations, which show improved reconstruction accuracy compared to traditional methods.

Theoretical studies have been conducted on the ionization characteristics of hydrogen atoms exposed to a high-frequency, bichromatic laser field. This laser field, which is circularly polarized, consists of two frequencies, omega1 and omega2, where omega1 is significantly higher than omega2. The research reveals that the ac-Stark shifts of the energy levels in the atom are directly proportional to the square of the intensity of the laser field. Furthermore, it has been observed that the high-order resonances in the photoelectron momentum spectrum are influenced by the difference in the frequencies of the two laser components.

The primary objective of image mixing techniques is to combine two images into a visually appealing output. However, existing methods primarily focus on image aesthetics, neglecting the semantic aspects. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel image mixing approach that not only considers the semantic content of images but also enhances the overall aesthetic quality of the output. Our method involves two stages: first, we utilize a pre-trained image encoder to extract the semantic content of input images, and then we employ a transformer-based model to generate the final output. To further improve the output quality, we incorporate a contrastive learning module that encourages the model to learn diverse image representations. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art image mixing techniques in terms of semantic and aesthetic quality.

The dynamics of gene expression are crucial for the development and function of organisms, and are influenced by a complex interplay of factors including the transcriptional machinery, regulatory elements, and external conditions. To understand this process, we must analyze the behavior of individual RNA molecules, which is often challenging due to the limitations of experimental techniques. To address this issue, we have developed a new approach that uses a combination of mathematical modeling and machine learning to extract meaningful information from noisy gene expression data. By applying this method to simulated data, we have demonstrated its effectiveness in identifying key features of gene expression, including the effects of regulatory elements and the presence of bursts. Furthermore, we have shown that our approach can be used to predict the behavior of genes in response to environmental changes, which is a critical aspect of understanding gene regulation.

In the realm of supervised learning, the availability of labeled data significantly impacts the model's performance. However, the process of obtaining these labels can be labor-intensive and costly, especially when dealing with complex datasets. This paper delves into the concept of semi-supervised learning, which utilizes a combination of labeled and unlabeled data to achieve better results. The primary goal of this approach is to minimize the reliance on labeled data while maximizing the model's performance. The proposed method, which is based on a data-driven approach, aims to identify the most critical labeled data points and eliminate the redundant ones. The model is then trained using the refined dataset, and the results are evaluated using the same data points. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on various datasets, and the code is made publicly available for further research and development.

A fundamental challenge in the field of quantum computing is developing a quantum algorithm that can efficiently solve complex problems. Quantum approximate optimization (QAOA) is a promising approach that uses a quantum computer to find approximate solutions to difficult optimization problems. This study focuses on the training of QAOA, specifically the "layerwise" method, which involves iteratively improving the quantum circuit's parameters. Our research reveals that this method can become stuck in a state of "training saturation," where further iterations do not yield improvements. We identify the underlying cause of this phenomenon as the circuit's Hamiltonian becoming increasingly similar to its initial state, which can be caused by the specific structure of the problem or the QAOA parameters. Our findings suggest that this similarity can be exploited to develop more efficient algorithms for solving complex optimization problems.

Person Re-Identification is a complex task that aims to identify individuals across different images. This problem has significant practical applications, such as tracking individuals across multiple cameras. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the state-of-the-art methods for Person Re-IDentification, covering both traditional and deep learning approaches. We examine the key factors that influence these methods, including data preprocessing, feature extraction, and matching techniques, and discuss their strengths and limitations. Furthermore, we discuss recent advancements in the field, including the use of deep learning and semi-supervised learning, and highlight potential areas for future research.

The increasing availability of modern power system data has led to a surge in research opportunities, enabling the development of innovative solutions for complex problems. This study presents a comprehensive dataset of 24-hour load distribution time series for 2,508 buses across 14 European countries, sourced from 10 different power system data initiatives. We utilize this dataset to investigate the impact of data quality on modern power system research, specifically focusing on the effects of data gaps and noise on time series forecasting. Our analysis reveals that data gaps and noise can significantly compromise the performance of time series forecasting models, emphasizing the need for high-quality data to support cutting-edge power system research.

This paper presents a novel algorithm, derived from the projected method, to solve a variational inequality problem. The algorithm's convergence properties are established, demonstrating that its limit is the problem's unique solution. The algorithm's ability to converge robustly to the problem's solution is also established, with its limit being unaffected by the algorithm's initial parameters. The algorithm's convergence properties are further validated through numerical testing.

We investigate the intersection patterns of geodesics within the hyperbolic triangle generated by three mutually orthogonal geodesics, which are part of a Fuchsian group's fundamental domain. This group is assumed to be non-uniform, non-arithmetic, and not congruental. By examining the geodesic configurations, we derive the complete set of Fuchsian groups that can be represented as isoxial groups. This involves identifying the specific triangle types associated with each geodesic configuration and determining the corresponding Fuchsian group.

A search for a rare flavor-changing decay in the $\Upsilon(3S)$ meson has been conducted, specifically examining the $\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\mp}$ transition. This investigation utilized $145$ fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider, where no significant evidence was found to support this decay. Consequently, upper limits were established on the branching ratio of this process, with values of $1.1\times10^{-6}$ and $1.3\times10^{-6}$ observed for $\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\mp}$ and $\Upsilon(3S)\rightarrow \mu^{\pm}\tau^{\mp}$ respectively. These results are the most stringent to date and have implications for our understanding of the Standard Model.

The Kagome lattice, a fundamental structure in condensed matter, has been a subject of interest for researchers due to its flat-band superconductivity. However, the high-pressure synthesis required to achieve this phase has hindered its study. Our research has led to the discovery of a new family of Kagome compounds, Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$, which can be synthesized at ambient pressure. By applying high pressure, we found that these compounds exhibit a superconducting phase, with the onset of superconductivity occurring at 1.5 K. Our findings suggest that the superconducting phase is a result of the pressure-induced flattening of the Fermi surface, a characteristic of the Kagome lattice.

We investigate the information recovery process of a three-dimensional black hole within the context of JT Gravity. By employing the Page curve to model the evolution of a black hole's entropy as it emits Hawking radiation, we demonstrate that the radiation's entropy is not solely a function of the black hole's mass, but also incorporates a non-trivial component. This non-trivial component is revealed to be a consequence of the radiation's entanglement entropy, which is influenced by the black hole's mass and a constant, $\beta_0$. Furthermore, we establish that the radiation's entanglement entropy is not solely a function of the black hole's mass, but also depends on the radiation's emission time.

Solving neural ordinary differential equations often relies on accurate measurements of the input and output data, which can be unreliable in real-world scenarios. This study focuses on neural ODEs that are trained using noisy data, demonstrating that they can still converge to the true solution under certain conditions. Furthermore, the research shows that neural ODEs can handle data with irregular time stamps, and provides a framework for estimating the solution's uncertainty. The findings are supported by experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, and have significant implications for the application of neural ODEs in complex systems.

The Object Goal Navigation task is a challenging problem in Reinforcement Learning that requires an agent to locate a target object within an environment. Current approaches often rely on pre-programmed object detection tools, which can be limited in their adaptability. In contrast, this research presents a novel method that enables the agent to learn and retain object information, thereby enhancing its navigation capabilities. By incorporating a Transformer-based object memory module, the agent can efficiently retrieve and utilize object features to guide its actions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showcasing its ability to surpass existing state-of-the-art navigation methods.

Recent advancements in instruction learning have led to significant improvements in few-shot task performance. However, the field has been plagued by a lack of understanding regarding the impact of instruction data on task performance. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the effects of instruction data on task performance. We propose OPT-IML, a novel approach that utilizes a pre-trained language model to learn instructions for various tasks. Our findings indicate that the quality of instruction data is crucial in determining task performance. Moreover, we discovered that the distribution of instruction data has a substantial influence on task performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel approach that involves generating a diverse set of instructions for each task. Our results demonstrate that OPT-IML can effectively utilize instruction data to enhance task performance.

The Scratch online community, centered around creating interactive content, has been a valuable resource for both children and adults since its inception in 2007. Initially designed to facilitate learning through hands-on experience, the platform has expanded to cater to diverse user needs. This study examines the various ways users engage with Scratch, identifying distinct levels of participation. Our analysis reveals that users' interactions with Scratch are influenced by their age, geographical location, and level of experience, leading to diverse engagement patterns. We also find that users' goals and motivations play a significant role in determining their level of involvement. Our research suggests that the concept of "legitimate peripheral participation" needs to be adapted to accommodate the diverse user experiences and goals within online communities.

The uniform electron gas is studied using a transcorrelated Hamiltonian, which is derived from a specific basis set. The transcorrelated Hamiltonian is then used to calculate the ground state energy of the system, with the basis set serving as an effective bath. The energy of the system is calculated using perturbation theory, with the result showing that the ground state energy of the system is a function of the density and the Coulomb coupling constant. The result is also compared to other effective Hamiltonians, with the result showing that the transcorrelated Hamiltonian is a more accurate representation of the system, with the result showing a higher accuracy in the calculation of the ground state energy.

We introduce a novel method for determining the optimal inflation factor for
uncertainty matrices in Bayesian inverse problems. This approach is grounded in
the concept of location uncertainty and utilizes optimal transportation
principles to quantify the uncertainty. The proposed method is applicable to a
broad range of inverse problems and can be applied to both linear and nonlinear
scenarios. Furthermore, our approach is physically informed, meaning that the
determined inflation factor adheres to the principles of the underlying physical
phenomena. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through numerical
experiments on linear and nonlinear inverse problems.

The widespread adoption of Big Data analytics has led to significant concerns regarding data privacy. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach for safeguarding sensitive information in large datasets. Our solution involves breaking down a large, complex dataset into smaller, decentralized tensors and distributing their components among multiple parties. Each party then applies a randomization algorithm to its respective tensor, effectively concealing sensitive data. To maintain data usability, we utilize a tensor network reconstruction algorithm, which can be applied by a third party to reassemble the original dataset under specific conditions. To demonstrate the efficacy of our method, we conducted a series of experiments on various datasets, which confirmed its ability to protect sensitive information while preserving data integrity.

In recent years, the use of simulation-based robot learning has gained significant traction. However, the process of translating learned policies directly to real-world robots poses a significant challenge due to the risk of accidents. To address this issue, researchers have developed the SafeAPT framework, which leverages the diversity of policies learned in simulated environments to ensure safe and efficient transfer to real-world robots. By utilizing a set of pre-trained policies, the framework employs a risk-averse reinforcement learning approach to identify a safe and effective policy for real-world robots. The proposed method has been successfully applied to the task of autonomous driving and has demonstrated its ability to achieve safe and efficient transfer to real-world robots.

Radio galaxies and quasars are characterized by powerful jets that are a key feature in their radio spectra. These jets are a crucial aspect of their physics, and their study has significantly advanced our understanding of their radio properties. This article provides an overview of the current state of knowledge about the radio properties of jets in radio galaxies and quasars.

This research focuses on developing a nonparametric framework for analyzing complex time series data within dynamic econometric models. By combining a time-adaptive regression model with a Markov switching mechanism, we create a dynamic framework that can be estimated using a novel sieve approach. Our method allows for the estimation of nonlinear relationships and time-heterogeneity within the data, while also enabling the derivation of asymptotic distributions for the resulting parameter estimates. Furthermore, we propose a new inference technique that can be used to accurately quantify the uncertainty surrounding these parameter estimates, even in the presence of non-stationarity.

The proliferation of online content has led to an increase in the use of abusive language, posing a significant challenge to social media platforms. This study focuses on identifying hate speech and offensive language, employing both traditional machine learning and neural network approaches. We examine the effectiveness of various feature extraction methods and classifier models, including the impact of using pre-trained word embeddings. Our analysis reveals that a neural network model, utilizing a convolutional neural network architecture, achieves a high accuracy rate of 0.93 in detecting offensive language, with a precision and recall of 0.92.

The brain's functional connections, which are reflected in the patterns of activity between different brain areas, can be difficult to measure directly. As a result, researchers often rely on indirect methods, such as analyzing the patterns of activity within a specific time frame or using a particular mathematical approach. However, these methods have limitations, and recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of new, more sophisticated techniques for analyzing brain data. In this study, we present a novel deep learning model that can be used to uncover the brain's functional connections, which we call the functional connectivity graph neural network (FCGNN). Our results show that this model outperforms existing methods, and we also demonstrate its ability to uncover novel functional connections that are not apparent using traditional approaches.

This paper presents a novel approach to understanding Nesterov's accelerated method through the lens of dissipativity theory. By doing so, we derive a fundamental inequality that underpins Nesterov's method and provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing its behavior. This framework enables us to establish a set of conditions that guarantee the convergence of Nesterov's method to a stable equilibrium point, and we demonstrate that these conditions are both necessary and sufficient. Furthermore, we show that Nesterov's method can be viewed as a discrete-time approximation of a continuous-time system, and we derive a set of conditions that ensure the existence of a stable equilibrium manifold for this system.

This research focuses on developing a boundary treatment for implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods applied to hyperbolic systems with non-linear, spatially-dependent source terms. A new approach is proposed, which involves a two-step process: first, solving a non-linear boundary value problem using a time-stepped solution, and then using an explicit stage computation to obtain the final solution. This method is shown to be stable under certain conditions, including a CFL condition and a boundary condition. Furthermore, the proposed approach is shown to be effective in numerical simulations, which demonstrate its stability and accuracy.

The development of thin-film solar cells is a key focus area in photovoltaics, 
with silicon films being a preferred choice due to their low cost and high
performance. However, thin films have lower absorption rates than thicker layers, 
which can be mitigated by using a reflective coating to increase light absorption. 
This study investigates the potential of a 3D photonic band gap back reflector to 
improve light absorption in thin silicon films, with a focus on optimizing its 
thickness and structure. The results show that this technology can significantly 
boost light absorption in thin films, with a 1.5 micron thick silicon film seeing 
a 20% increase in absorption.

This paper introduces a novel framework called Credal Valuation Networks (CVNs) for modeling complex systems under uncertainty. CVNs leverage the capabilities of credal sets, a type of imprecise probability model, to represent uncertainty within the network. The CVN framework extends traditional valuation networks by incorporating credal set representations on each node, allowing for the propagation of uncertainty through the network. The paper outlines a systematic approach for computing the tightest bounds of the network's output credal set, given the input distributions. The proposed method is demonstrated through a case study in medical diagnosis.

The task of Top-K recommendation involves identifying the most relevant items for a given query within a set of options. Traditional methods for addressing this challenge rely on pairwise ranking, which, however, often overlook the broader context of the query. In contrast, our proposed approach, Probabilistic Metric Learning with Adaptive Margin (PML-AM), employs a probabilistic model that considers the relationships between the query and its surrounding items. By incorporating a flexible margin, our model can effectively capture the nuances of the recommendation context. Furthermore, our method is computationally efficient, allowing for seamless integration into existing Top-K recommendation frameworks. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, which outperforms existing methods in terms of recommendation accuracy.

We investigate the occurrence of non-Markovianity in a broad category of non-unital quantum channels, which cannot be represented as a combination of unital quantum channels. Our analysis reveals that these channels can exhibit non-Markovian behavior, and we develop a method to identify this phenomenon. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method can be used to detect non-Markovianity in any quantum system, regardless of its dimension. Additionally, we examine the relationship between non-Markovianity and the concept of eternal return, and we provide a specific example of a non-unital channel that remains non-Markovian for all time.

In the context of machine learning, active learning has garnered significant attention as a means to optimize the training process by strategically selecting the most informative samples. This research focuses on developing an active learning framework that incorporates counterfactual reasoning to enhance the efficiency of classification models. The proposed approach, dubbed CFA, combines the strengths of contrastive learning and active learning to achieve improved performance. The CFA framework is evaluated on various datasets, demonstrating its ability to achieve comparable results with significantly reduced training samples.

A key component in the development of autonomous robots is the creation of detailed maps that accurately represent their surroundings. To achieve this, robots must be able to detect and interpret the world around them, including both its visual appearance and physical structure. To evaluate the effectiveness of these robots, a comprehensive benchmarking system is necessary, capable of assessing their performance in a variety of scenarios. To address this need, we introduce RoSmEEry, a comprehensive simulation environment designed to test and evaluate the capabilities of semantic mapping algorithms. RoSmEEry is built using Gazebo, a widely-used simulation tool, and includes a range of pre-defined scenarios that challenge the robot's mapping abilities. To demonstrate the potential of RoSmEEry, we conduct a series of experiments using the OpenCV SLAM library, and show that our proposed approach can produce high-quality maps even in complex environments.

Rikudo is a well-known Japanese board game, and its computational complexity has been a subject of research. In this study, we demonstrate that Rikudo is indeed complex enough to require non-trivial solutions, and its decision-making process cannot be efficiently solved even with basic algorithms. Furthermore, we establish that Rikudo is closely related to another complex game, Go-Endo, and its complexity can be used to improve our understanding of the game's strategies.

Optimal transport has gained significant attention in the fields of machine learning and statistics, primarily due to its ability to quantify the difference between probability measures. The emergence of efficient algorithms for solving optimal transport problems has enabled the development of more sophisticated methods for analyzing and understanding complex data sets. This thesis focuses on the development of numerical techniques for solving large-scale optimal transport problems, with a particular emphasis on the use of entropy-regularized optimal transport. The thesis begins by examining the relationship between entropy-regularized optimal transport and gradient descent, leading to the derivation of a novel algorithm for solving optimal transport problems. The algorithm's convergence is rigorously established, and its performance is demonstrated through numerical experiments. The thesis then explores the application of optimal transport in the field of machine learning, specifically through the lens of generative modeling. The use of optimal transport for learning probabilistic generative models is investigated, with a focus on the development of a novel generative model that leverages optimal transport to learn the distribution of a data set. The thesis concludes by examining the application of optimal transport in the context of reinforcement learning, with a focus on the use of optimal transport to learn the distribution of a Markov chain. The thesis presents a novel algorithm for learning the distribution of a Markov chain using optimal transport, and demonstrates its performance through numerical experiments.

Ramanujan's work on modular equations has been a significant area of influence, 
with Hecke building upon these ideas to establish the Hecke groups and their 
subgroups, such as the unimodular subgroup, which has been further explored 
by subsequent researchers.

We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of eight gravitationally lensed quasars using Keck spectroscopy, which has yielded new redshift and velocity dispersion measurements for the lensing galaxies. Our findings are based on a combination of echelle spectroscopy and long-slit spectroscopy, and we have employed a novel method to determine the velocity dispersion of the lensing galaxies. This involves analyzing the absorption lines of the quasars and comparing them to the absorption lines of the lensing galaxies. Our results are consistent with previous measurements for six of the lensing galaxies, and we have obtained new measurements for the remaining two systems. Our analysis has also revealed that the velocity dispersion of the lensing galaxies is correlated with their redshift, and we have compared our findings to the predictions of the dark matter halo evolution model. Our results suggest that the lensing galaxies are consistent with the predictions of the model, and we have also explored the implications of our findings for the properties of the lensed quasars.

This paper presents a new approach to solving nonlinear fractional differential equations on the $q$-factional chain time scale via a difference method. We introduce a new concept of $q$-fractional difference for functions on the $q$-factional chain time scale and establish the properties of $q$-fractional difference operators. We then develop a difference scheme for a nonlinear fractional differential equation and prove its stability. Furthermore, we demonstrate the convergence of the difference scheme to the original solution. Additionally, we provide a numerical example to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

A new phenomenon, the phonon Hall effect, has been discovered in a specific material, where acoustic waves behave like electrons in a magnetic field. This effect is observed in a particular material, but it can also occur in other materials with the same properties. The research shows that the phonon Hall effect is related to a specific geometric structure, and its behavior can be explained by how the material's properties change with frequency. The effect is not unique to this material, but it can occur in other materials with the same properties, and it may also be observed in certain wave-based materials.

A novel, wide-field imaging technique has been developed to capture the Raman spectrum of molecules at the single-cell or single-protein level. This technique, called Shifted Excitation Raman Difference Spectroscopy (SERDS), involves exciting the sample with two distinct wavelengths and measuring the resulting Raman spectrum. By using the Nod and Shuffle technique, researchers can efficiently collect data from large areas, achieving high spatial resolution and speed. This method has been successfully demonstrated in various applications, including the imaging of cells and tissues.

We derive matrix analogues of Fejér and Levin-Stečkin inequalities for a specific class of matrices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain matrix inequalities are equivalent to the matrix Fejér inequality.

We investigate the average null energy condition for a black hole that is losing its energy due to evaporation. Our analysis focuses on the average null energy within a specific region of the event horizon, specifically the area outside the apparent horizon. We find that this condition holds true for a certain range of parameters, but it is violated when the evaporation rate exceeds a specific threshold. This threshold is determined by the mass of the black hole and its lifetime. Our results also show that the average null energy within the specified region approaches zero as the evaporation process nears its end.
